Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be signed measures or complex measures on the same
measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. They are **mutually singular**, written
$$\mu\perp \nu,$$
when there are measurable sets $P,N\in\mathcal A$ with
$$P\cap N=\varnothing,\qquad P\cup N=X,$$
such that:

1. every measurable subset of $N$ has $\mu$-value $0$;
2. every measurable subset of $P$ has $\nu$-value $0$.

For positive measures this is equivalent to the usual condition
$\mu(N)=0$ and $\nu(P)=0$, because positivity turns vanishing on the ambient set
into vanishing on all measurable subsets.

Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on the same measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. We say that $
u$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$**, and write
$$
u\ll\mu,$$
if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $
u$-null:
$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
u(E)=0\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $
u(F)=0$ for every measurable $F\subseteq E$ whenever $\mu(E)=0$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

derivations.claim:
Choose the singular carrier $N$ from [F1]. For any measurable $E$, the singular part vanishes on $E\setminus N$, so the decomposition gives $
u_{\mathrm{ac}}(E\setminus N)=
u(E\setminus N)\ge0$. Also $
u_{\mathrm{ac}}(E\cap N)=0$ by [F1] and [F2]. Additivity therefore gives $
u_{\mathrm{ac}}(E)=
u_{\mathrm{ac}}(E\setminus N)\ge0$. All displayed component values are finite because the sum is the finite value $
u$ and the other component is zero on the set being evaluated.

On $E\cap N$, [F2] gives $
u_{\mathrm{ac}}(E\cap N)=0$, so the decomposition yields $
u_{\mathrm{s}}(E\cap N)=
u(E\cap N)\ge0$. The singular part vanishes on $E\setminus N$ by [F1]; hence $
u_{\mathrm{s}}(E)=
u_{\mathrm{s}}(E\cap N)\ge0$. Since $E$ was arbitrary, both components are positive measures.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already
suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into
the definition here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure.

1. If $\nu$ is a signed measure satisfying the hypothesis of [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]] and $\nu\ll\mu$, the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** $d\nu/d\mu$ is the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equivalence class of measurable real-valued functions $f$ satisfying the measurable-set integral formula in that theorem.
2. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), if $\nu$ is a finite complex measure and $\nu\ll\mu$, the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** $d\nu/d\mu$ is the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equivalence class of complex $L^1(\mu)$ functions $h$ satisfying
   $$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A),$$
   as given by [[cor-finite-complex-measures-admit-integrable-radon-nikodym-densities]].

In both cases the derivative is not a distinguished pointwise function: it is determined only up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality in the sense of [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]].

Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on the same measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. We say that $
u$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$**, and write
$$
u\ll\mu,$$
if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $
u$-null:
$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
u(E)=0\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $
u(F)=0$ for every measurable $F\subseteq E$ whenever $\mu(E)=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim:
Choose increasing countable finite-measure covers $(A_i)$ for $\mu$ and $(B_j)$ for $
u$, using [F1]. Set $X_n= igcup_{i,j\le n}(A_i\cap B_j)$. Then $X_n\uparrow X$ and both $\mu(X_n)$ and $
u(X_n)$ are finite, since each finite union is contained in finite unions of sets from the corresponding cover. By [F2], $|
u|(X_n)=
u(X_n)<\infty$. Thus [F3] applies. Fix any finite-valued representative $f$ of the nonempty class; it satisfies $
u(E)=\int_E f\,d\mu$ for every measurable $E$ and $\int_{X_n}|f|\,d\mu<\infty$.

For $n,m\ge1$, let $E_{n,m}=X_n\cap\{f\le-1/m\}$, which is measurable by [F5]. On $E_{n,m}$, $-f\ge1/m$; because $f$ is integrable on $X_n$, [F6] and [F7] give $\int_{E_{n,m}}f\,d\mu\le-\mu(E_{n,m})/m$. If $\mu(E_{n,m})>0$, the representation in step 1.1 would give $\nu(E_{n,m})<0$, contradicting positivity of $\nu$. Hence every $E_{n,m}$ is $\mu$-null.
The countable union $N=\bigcup_{n,m\ge1}E_{n,m}$ is measurable and $\mu$-null by [F5]. Since the sets $X_n$ cover $X$, $N=\{f<0\}$.

Define $\widetilde f=\max\{f,0\}$. By [F7], $\widetilde f$ is measurable; it is nonnegative, equals $f$ off $N$, and is zero on $N$. For every measurable $E$, absolute continuity gives $
u(E)=
u(E\setminus N)$ by [F4], while step 1.1 gives $
u(E\setminus N)=\int_{E\setminus N}f\,d\mu=\int_E\widetilde f\,d\mu$. Thus $\widetilde f$ represents the Radon–Nikodym class. The argument also shows that any finite-valued representative is nonnegative outside a null set.

$P_1=P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}+P_{1,\mathrm{s}}$ with

absolutely continuous case $P_1\ll P_0$. If that condition fails, the

measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $P_0$ and $P_1$ be probability measures on the same measurable space.
Assume AC. Their Lebesgue decomposition relative to $P_0$ is the unique
decomposition
$P_1=P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}+P_{1,\mathrm{s}}$ with
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}\ll P_0$ and $P_{1,\mathrm{s}}\perp P_0$
([[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-exists-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]],
[[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-is-unique-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]]).
Both components are positive by
[[lem-positive-lebesgue-components-of-a-positive-measure]], and
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}$ is finite because their sum has mass one. Define the
**likelihood-ratio density** of $P_1$ against $P_0$ to be the
$P_0$-almost-everywhere class
$$
\frac{dP_{1,\mathrm{ac}}}{dP_0}
$$
of [[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]. Under AC this class has a nonnegative
measurable representative by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

This is a full density of $P_1$ with respect to $P_0$ only in the
absolutely continuous case $P_1\ll P_0$. If that condition fails, the
singular component remains separate. A displayed representative is not a
canonical pointwise function: its values are determined only
$P_0$-almost everywhere.

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The full power set is a sigma-algebra by [F1], so [F2] gives a measurable space. The counting measure is finite with $\mu(\mathcal X)=2$ by [F3], hence sigma-finite. Each displayed mass is nonnegative and the two masses for each $P_i$ sum to $1$. For any disjoint sequence of events, each point belongs to at most one event, so the mass formula is countably additive; each $P_i$ is therefore a probability measure by [F4]. Since counting measure assigns positive mass to every nonempty subset, $P_i\ll\mu$, and the family is a dominated experiment by [F5]–[F6].

Put $p_i(x):=P_i(\{x\})$ for $i\in\{0,1\}$. For every $A\subseteq\mathcal X$, $\int_A p_i\,d\mu=\sum_{x\in A}p_i(x)=P_i(A)$, so these are density representatives as in [F7]. Since $p_0$ is positive at both points, $P_1\ll P_0$; define $r(x)=p_1(x)/p_0(x)$. For every $A\subseteq\mathcal X$, $\int_A r\,dP_0=\sum_{x\in A}r(x)p_0(x)=\sum_{x\in A}p_1(x)=P_1(A)$; thus $r$ represents the likelihood-ratio derivative [F8], with $r(0)=(1/3)/(2/3)=1/2$ and $r(1)=(2/3)/(1/3)=2$. [A1, F7, F8, given, algebra]

For any real-valued $g$ on $\mathcal X$, $E_{P_0}[gr]=\frac23g(0)\frac12+\frac13g(1)2=\frac13g(0)+\frac23g(1)=E_{P_1}[g]$. Thus the change-of-measure identity holds directly, in agreement with [A1, F9].
